subject: combined-science
title: Chemistry — Electrolysis
meta_desc: GCSE Combined Science (AQA) practice covering Chemistry — Electrolysis, specification section 4.4.3.
final_note: You worked through Chemistry — Electrolysis — 22 specification statements.

concepts.def: An ionic compound that has been melted or dissolved in water, so that its ions are free to move about within the liquid or solution. Electrolytes conduct electricity.
The process in which passing an electric current through an electrolyte makes the ions move to the electrodes, where they are discharged to produce elements.
The negative electrode. Positively charged ions move to it.
The positive electrode. Negatively charged ions move to it.
An electrode, such as graphite or platinum, that does not take part in the reactions of the cell, so the products come only from the electrolyte.
The loss of charge by an ion at an electrode, as electrons are gained or lost, turning the ion into a neutral atom or molecule of an element.
An ionic compound made of just two elements, one metal and one non-metal, such as lead bromide or magnesium chloride.

concepts.term: Products of a molten binary compound
concepts.def: When a molten binary ionic compound is electrolysed with inert electrodes, the metal is produced at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode.
Obtaining a metal from its molten compound by electrolysis. It is used when the metal is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon, or when the metal reacts with carbon.
Large amounts of energy are used in extraction by electrolysis, both to melt the compound and to produce the electrical current.
The compound mixed with aluminium oxide in the aluminium cell. The mixture melts at a lower temperature than aluminium oxide alone, so less energy is needed.
The positive electrode is made of carbon. Oxygen produced there reacts with the hot carbon, so the electrode is worn away and must be replaced continually.
At the negative electrode hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen; otherwise the metal is produced.
At the positive electrode oxygen is produced unless the solution contains halide ions, when the halogen is produced.
In an aqueous solution water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions, and these ions can be discharged at the electrodes.
A testable idea, put forward before the experiment, that predicts what will happen and can be supported or disproved by the results of Required practical 3.
Gain of electrons. At the cathode positively charged ions gain electrons, so the reactions there are reductions.
Loss of electrons. At the anode negatively charged ions lose electrons, so the reactions there are oxidations.
An equation showing the reaction at one electrode only, including the electrons gained or lost, balanced for both atoms and charge.
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻, which may also be written as 4OH⁻ – 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O.
A lit splint gives a squeaky pop with hydrogen. A glowing splint relights in oxygen, and damp litmus paper is bleached by chlorine.

mcqs.q: Solid lead bromide does not conduct electricity, but molten lead bromide does. Why?
options: Melting changes the neutral atoms into charged ions
Melting releases electrons that then carry the charge
Melting frees the ions so they can move through the liquid
Solid lead bromide contains no charged particles
mcqs.explain: Conduction needs charges free to move; melting breaks up the lattice and the ions move about within the liquid.

mcqs.q: Which of these can act as an electrolyte?
options: Sodium chloride dissolved in pure water
Sodium chloride kept as a dry white solid
A copper wire carrying an electric current
Sugar dissolved in some warm water
mcqs.explain: Dissolving separates the ions and lets them move about in the solution, so the solution conducts.

mcqs.q: During electrolysis, where do the positively charged ions move to?
options: To the positive electrode, which attracts them
To the anode, which is the negative electrode
To the anode, where they give up electrons
To the cathode, the negative electrode
mcqs.explain: Opposite charges attract, so positive ions move to the negative electrode, which is called the cathode.

mcqs.q: Ions are discharged at the electrodes during electrolysis. What is produced?
options: New compounds that build up on each electrode
Elements, as the ions lose their charge
The original compound, moved to the electrodes
Electrons, which flow back out into the wire
mcqs.explain: Discharge removes the charge from an ion, leaving neutral atoms that make up an element.

mcqs.q: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What is produced at the cathode?
options: Bromine, because the non-metals form there
Lead, the metal, collects at the cathode
Hydrogen, made from water in this melt
Lead ions, Pb²⁺, coating the whole electrode
mcqs.explain: Lead ions are positive, so they move to the negative electrode and are discharged as lead metal.

mcqs.q: What is seen at the anode when molten lead bromide is electrolysed?
options: A silvery bead of molten lead collects on it
Colourless oxygen gas bubbles away from it
Bromide ions are given off as a brown gas
Orange-brown bromine vapour is given off
mcqs.explain: Bromide ions are negative, move to the anode and are discharged there as bromine.

mcqs.q: Molten magnesium chloride is electrolysed. Which products are formed?
options: Magnesium at the negative electrode and chlorine at the positive
Chlorine at the negative electrode, magnesium at the positive
Hydrogen at the negative electrode and chlorine at the positive
Magnesium at the negative electrode and oxygen at the positive
mcqs.explain: The metal ion is positive so magnesium forms at the cathode; chloride ions are negative so chlorine forms at the anode.

mcqs.q: Molten aluminium oxide is electrolysed. Which products are formed?
options: Hydrogen at the cathode, oxygen at the anode
Oxygen at the cathode with aluminium at the anode
Aluminium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Aluminium ions at the cathode, oxide ions at the anode
mcqs.explain: Aluminium ions are positive and are discharged at the cathode; oxide ions are negative and give oxygen at the anode.

mcqs.q: Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis rather than by reduction with carbon?
options: Electrolysis is the cheaper of the two methods
Carbon needs a higher temperature than the furnace reaches
Aluminium is too reactive to be reduced by carbon
Carbon would leave the metal much too impure to use
mcqs.explain: Carbon only removes oxygen from the oxides of metals less reactive than carbon; aluminium is above it.

mcqs.q: Why does extracting a metal by electrolysis use so much energy?
options: The ore must first be purified using costly chemicals
Energy is needed to melt the compound and produce the current
Electrolysis needs far more ore than reduction by carbon
Most of the energy is used to mine the ore from the ground
mcqs.explain: Large amounts of energy are used both to melt the compound and to produce the electrical current.

mcqs.q: In the manufacture of aluminium, what is the electrolyte and what is the positive electrode made of?
options: Aluminium oxide dissolved in warm water, with a steel anode
Molten cryolite on its own, with an anode made of carbon
Solid aluminium oxide packed around the carbon anode
A molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite, carbon anode
mcqs.explain: The specification states a molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite with carbon as the positive electrode.

mcqs.q: Why is cryolite mixed with the aluminium oxide?
options: It lowers the melting point, so less energy is needed
It acts as a catalyst and speeds the process up
It supplies all the aluminium ions that are discharged
It stops the hot aluminium reacting with the air
mcqs.explain: Aluminium oxide alone melts at a very high temperature; the mixture melts lower, saving energy.

mcqs.q: Why must the positive electrode in the aluminium cell be replaced continually?
options: Oxygen made there reacts with the carbon and wears it away
The heat of the molten mixture slowly melts the carbon
The carbon dissolves in the melt because it is positive
Aluminium coats the carbon and stops it conducting
mcqs.explain: Oxygen is discharged at the anode and reacts with the hot carbon, so the electrode is eaten away.

mcqs.q: When an aqueous solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes, what decides which ions are discharged?
options: The size of the charge carried by each of the ions
The mass of each of the ions present in the solution
The metal is discharged whatever else is there
The relative reactivity of the elements involved
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the ions discharged depend on the relative reactivity of the elements involved.

mcqs.q: Copper chloride solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?
options: Hydrogen, because copper is less reactive than it
Copper, as it is less reactive than hydrogen
Chlorine, since chloride ions are drawn there
Oxygen, released as the water breaks apart
mcqs.explain: The less reactive element is discharged, and copper is below hydrogen in reactivity.

mcqs.q: Sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?
options: Sodium, because it is the metal in the compound used
Sulfur, which forms from the sulfate ions in solution
Hydrogen, as sodium is more reactive than hydrogen
Oxygen, which the water always gives off there
mcqs.explain: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions from the water are discharged instead.

mcqs.q: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the anode?
options: Sodium, which is drawn to the positive electrode
Hydrogen, coming from the water in the solution
Oxygen, which always forms at that electrode
Chlorine, as the solution holds halide ions
mcqs.explain: Oxygen is produced at the anode unless the solution contains halide ions, when the halogen is produced.

mcqs.q: Copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the anode?
options: Oxygen, as no halide ions are present
Sulfur dioxide, made from the sulfate ions
Copper, plating onto the positive electrode
Hydrogen, from the breakdown of the water
mcqs.explain: Sulfate is not a halide, so hydroxide ions from the water are discharged and oxygen is produced.

mcqs.q: In the electrolysis of an aqueous solution, where do the hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions come from?
options: From the dissolved compound splitting into its ions
From water molecules that break down in the solution
From hydrogen and oxygen gas dissolved in water
From the electrodes, which release them into the liquid
mcqs.explain: In the aqueous solution water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions.

mcqs.q: A student plans Required practical 3 and writes an idea down before starting. Which statement is a hypothesis the investigation could test?
options: Copper chloride solution is a clear blue liquid
Bubbles appeared at the negative electrode
Solutions of halides will give a halogen at the anode
Which gas is given off at the negative electrode?
mcqs.explain: It is a testable prediction, made in advance, that the results of the practical can support or disprove.

mcqs.q: In Required practical 3, the gas collected at the cathode gave a squeaky pop with a lit splint. What does this show?
options: Hydrogen formed, so the metal is more reactive
Oxygen formed, because oxygen relights the splint
Chlorine formed, since it bleaches damp litmus paper
The metal itself formed and burned with the lit splint
mcqs.explain: A squeaky pop identifies hydrogen, which is discharged when the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.

mcqs.q: At the cathode, positively charged ions gain electrons. How is this reaction described?
options: Oxidation, because the electrons are gained
Reduction, because electrons are gained
Oxidation, as the cathode is negative
Neutralisation, as the charge has gone
mcqs.explain: Reduction is gain of electrons, so reactions at the cathode are reductions.

mcqs.q: At the anode, negatively charged ions lose electrons. How is this reaction described?
options: Reduction, because electrons are lost
Reduction, since the anode is positive
Oxidation, as electrons are lost by the ions
Oxidation, because oxygen is always made here
mcqs.explain: Oxidation is loss of electrons, so reactions at the anode are oxidations.

mcqs.q: Which pair of half equations represents the reactions at the two electrodes correctly?
options: 2H⁺ → H₂ + 2e⁻ at the cathode and 4OH⁻ + 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O at the anode
H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂ at the cathode and OH⁻ → O₂ + H₂O + e⁻ at the anode
4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ at the cathode, 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ at the anode
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ at the cathode, and 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ at the anode
mcqs.explain: Positive ions gain electrons at the cathode and negative ions lose electrons at the anode; both equations balance.

mcqs.q: Which half equation shows hydrogen being produced at the cathode?
options: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
2H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂
H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂
mcqs.explain: Two hydrogen ions gain two electrons to form one molecule of hydrogen; atoms and charge both balance.

mcqs.q: Which half equation shows hydroxide ions being discharged at the anode?
options: 4OH⁻ → 2O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
2OH⁻ + 2e⁻ → O₂ + H₂O
OH⁻ → O₂ + H₂O + e⁻
4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
mcqs.explain: Four hydroxide ions lose four electrons, giving one molecule of oxygen and two of water; atoms and charge balance.

mcqs.q: The anode reaction may be written as 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ or as 4OH⁻ – 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O. How are the two related?
options: The second one supplies electrons instead of removing them
The first is the anode one, the second the cathode one
They are the same reaction, written in two ways
The second one applies to a molten compound only
mcqs.explain: Losing four electrons can be shown by subtracting them on the left or adding them on the right.

mcqs.q: Complete and balance the half equation for the reaction at the cathode in the aluminium cell.
options: 3Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → 3Al
Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al
Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → 3Al
Al³⁺ + e⁻ → Al
mcqs.explain: Each aluminium ion carries three positive charges, so it gains three electrons to form an aluminium atom.

mcqs.q: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed. Which half equation shows the reaction at the cathode?
options: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb
Pb²⁺ + e⁻ → Pb
2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻
2Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2Pb
mcqs.explain: Each lead ion carries two positive charges, so it gains two electrons at the cathode to form a lead atom.

mcqs.q: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed. Which half equation shows the reaction at the anode?
options: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
2Cl⁻ + 2e⁻ → Cl₂
2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 4e⁻
2Na⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2Na
mcqs.explain: Two chloride ions each lose one electron at the anode, giving one molecule of chlorine; atoms and charge balance.
